sources.title: Meta is working on making Muse its smart glasses assistant - Android Authority
passages: Meta is preparing to make its new AI agent Muse the brains behind its smart glasses, potentially replacing the standard Meta AI with a significantly more autonomous assistant.
A separate leak shared by Wong on X shows Meta is also working on “Meta Pay for Muse,” developing a native wallet interface for Muse with Meta Pay support, alongside Stripe’s Link and Shop Pay.
The integration appears designed to enable the agent to execute real-world transactions and make secure purchases on a user’s behalf.

The leaked setup screen, titled “Enable Impacc as your glasses assistant?” (where “Impacc” likely refers to an internal codename for Muse), notes that Muse is in beta and will allow users to swap back to Meta AI whenever they prefer.

Interestingly, the prompt explicitly lists features that are not yet available in the beta, tipping Meta’s hand on what is coming: Live AI, Navigation, Shazam song identification, Strava, and Health Connect integrations.
The move fits cleanly alongside Meta’s broader hardware roadmap.
The company currently dominates the market for smart-glasses shipments , and recent reports indicate it is exploring camera-free smart glasses focused entirely on ambient voice interactions .
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission.

Adding turn-by-turn navigation and fitness-tracking capabilities would transform Meta’s eyewear from a passive conversational accessory into an active, hands-free personal enabler device, just like your phone.
Wearers could perhaps track a run in Strava or ask the glasses to guide them home entirely by voice.

sources.title: Meta's Muse AI Agent Is Coming To Its AI Glasses - Engadget
passages: If you're willing to trust it with the most sensitive parts of your digital life, it can use the web, book travel, make phone calls, send emails and even make purchases on your behalf.
So far, you can use Muse in its standalone iOS, Android or Mac apps, or within your WhatsApp chats.
But in "the coming months," Meta is bringing its errand-running agent to its AI glasses.
But that gets to a question about how much Muse for glasses really adds: agentic AI's appeal is that it does things in the background without constant supervision.
Pulling out your phone to give it a new task doesn't exactly sound like much of a burden.
The glasses do make that hands-free, and Meta suggested some situations where that could be useful: guiding personalized workouts, logging meals and providing nutritional insights.
But that sounds like more of a convenience than a necessity.
Meta shared more details about Muse for AI glasses at its Connect 2026 event on Wednesday.

The company said Muse will help you "stay on top of things, take tasks and projects off your plate and turn long-term goals into action plans, all hands-free." Specific examples include booking appointments, checking flight prices and tracking down items.

But that sounds like more of a convenience than a necessity. Still, if you're investing in the privacy-threatening "perv glasses" anyway, you may as well get Meta's new personal AI agent to go with them, right?

sources.title: Everything new coming to Meta’s AI agent Muse - TechCrunch
passages: Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”
Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.
The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars.
At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.

extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date. CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives. “The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta. “We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said. Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions. Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see. Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done. It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.” Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop. “You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.” Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline. Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf. Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping. Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal. The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion. Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.” Anthropic releases Opus 5.5 with lower prices and Fable-level performance Russell Brandom Meta’s Muse is outpacing ChatGPT’s early mobile launch Sarah Perez Tilly Norwood’s press tour is going about as well as you’d expect for an AI Amanda Silberling Anthropic is operating a lab that conducts biology experiments Julie Bort A new kind of AI model from a ChatGPT inventor is thrilling developers Tim Fernholz OpenAI caught its models leaving notes to successors to hide bad behavior Rebecca Bellan

One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says.

The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions.

Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see.

“You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.”

They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses.
A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side.
The Meta Ray-Ban Display will also start using “the world in front of you rather than street signs in turn-by-turn walking directions,” like referencing a house, car, or landmark the glasses detect.

extraction.body: Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it’s “working on” bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they’re looking at. Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta’s glasses. They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses. Meta AI will also be able to give “more context-rich answers” when users ask the glasses what they’re looking at, potentially making Meta’s glasses more effective for helping blind and low-vision users interpret their surroundings. A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side. Meta’s introducing some new audio and photo features as well, including Dolby Atmos Capture, which will allow users to record videos with 360-degree spatial audio. A new Dynamic Photo feature automatically captures multiple frames when you take a photo with Meta’s glasses, then uses Meta AI to suggest the best frame from each batch. The Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are getting the new “Hologram” feature Meta announced for its new VR Glasses, which it says is “a photorealistic digital version of your face for calls from Meta Ray-Ban Display” that “infers” your expression using your voice. The feature’s “rolling out in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.” A couple new heads-up navigation features are coming to the Meta Ray-Ban Display as well. The Meta Ray-Ban Display will also start using “the world in front of you rather than street signs in turn-by-turn walking directions,” like referencing a house, car, or landmark the glasses detect. A few other new features are on the way for the Display glasses, including an option for editing photos directly on the glasses’ display, a new “Explore” app for finding new apps, an improved calendar, and mirroring for phone notifications.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta is preparing to make its new AI agent Muse the brains behind its smart glasses, potentially replacing the standard Meta AI with a significantly more autonomous assistant.
A separate leak shared by Wong on X shows Meta is also working on “Meta Pay for Muse,” developing a native wallet interface for Muse with Meta Pay support, alongside Stripe’s Link and Shop Pay.
The integration appears designed to enable the agent to execute real-world transactions and make secure purchases on a user’s behalf.

The leaked setup screen, titled “Enable Impacc as your glasses assistant?” (where “Impacc” likely refers to an internal codename for Muse), notes that Muse is in beta and will allow users to swap back to Meta AI whenever they prefer.

Interestingly, the prompt explicitly lists features that are not yet available in the beta, tipping Meta’s hand on what is coming: Live AI, Navigation, Shazam song identification, Strava, and Health Connect integrations.
The move fits cleanly alongside Meta’s broader hardware roadmap.
The company currently dominates the market for smart-glasses shipments , and recent reports indicate it is exploring camera-free smart glasses focused entirely on ambient voice interactions .
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission.

Adding turn-by-turn navigation and fitness-tracking capabilities would transform Meta’s eyewear from a passive conversational accessory into an active, hands-free personal enabler device, just like your phone.
Wearers could perhaps track a run in Strava or ask the glasses to guide them home entirely by voice.
If you're willing to trust it with the most sensitive parts of your digital life, it can use the web, book travel, make phone calls, send emails and even make purchases on your behalf.
So far, you can use Muse in its standalone iOS, Android or Mac apps, or within your WhatsApp chats.
But in "the coming months," Meta is bringing its errand-running agent to its AI glasses.
But that gets to a question about how much Muse for glasses really adds: agentic AI's appeal is that it does things in the background without constant supervision.
Pulling out your phone to give it a new task doesn't exactly sound like much of a burden.
The glasses do make that hands-free, and Meta suggested some situations where that could be useful: guiding personalized workouts, logging meals and providing nutritional insights.
But that sounds like more of a convenience than a necessity.
Meta shared more details about Muse for AI glasses at its Connect 2026 event on Wednesday.

The company said Muse will help you "stay on top of things, take tasks and projects off your plate and turn long-term goals into action plans, all hands-free." Specific examples include booking appointments, checking flight prices and tracking down items.
Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.

passages: If you're willing to trust it with the most sensitive parts of your digital life, it can use the web, book travel, make phone calls, send emails and even make purchases on your behalf.
So far, you can use Muse in its standalone iOS, Android or Mac apps, or within your WhatsApp chats.
But in "the coming months," Meta is bringing its errand-running agent to its AI glasses.
But that gets to a question about how much Muse for glasses really adds: agentic AI's appeal is that it does things in the background without constant supervision.
Pulling out your phone to give it a new task doesn't exactly sound like much of a burden.

extraction.body: "No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent," the talent agency said in a statement Wednesday night. Meta , led by CEO and AI enthusiast Mark Zuckerberg, this week rolled out the first photo and video tools to come out of its Superintelligence Labs: Muse Photo and Muse Video. The tool brings Meta in line with the state of the art in AI media creation, alongside Google’s Gemini and Seedance 2.0, but along with the tools, Meta also said that all public Instagram profiles will be opt-out, not opt-in, and other users can pull in those other accounts that don’t opt out and create new content using their profiles. For celebrities and other high-profile figures, that could be a major problem, even if most do end up opting out. Now Creative Artists Agency is calling out Meta for the move, and asking the tech giant to make it opt-in, not opt-out. “No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent. True innovation puts creators first: respecting their rights, protecting their livelihoods, and giving them real control, not handing it over to platforms,” CAA said in a statement Wednesday evening. “We have raised our concerns with Meta on behalf of our clients, voicing our disapproval and perspective on the need for a more responsible approach. We call on Meta to make protection the default on Muse Image, not the exception, and enable individuals to opt-in if they want to allow usage of their image or likeness for AI content creation. “Artists deserve to decide if and how their likeness and work is used, with consent and the ability to set their own terms,” the statement continues. “This means letting creators impose restrictions, monitor usage, and prevent unauthorized endorsements or exploitation. Responsible AI requires clear disclosures and swift removal of unauthorized content. There must be easy ways to spot, track, and take down misuse, and it should be clear when something is AI-generated. CAA believes in the power of new technology, but not at the cost of individuals’ rights or livelihoods. The future of creativity depends on respecting the ownership and autonomy of those who make it possible.” CAA, of course, is well aware of the opportunities and threats posed by generative AI to its clients. The agency maintains what it calls the “CAA Vault,” where the digital likenesses of its clients reside for potential future monetization and protection, and the agency was the first test user of YouTube’s deepfake detection tool, which rolled out to all of Hollywood earlier this year. The Muse situation is reminiscent of the botches launch of OpenAI’s Sora, which was overrun with well-known IP and the likenesses of many high-profile figures, forcing the AI giant to pivot to an opt-in model, before it scrapped the video model altogether earlier this year. After Sora launched, WME said that it was opting out on behalf of all of its clients, the first domino to fall in that model’s short life. “There is a strong need for real protections for artists and creatives as they encounter AI models using their intellectual property, as well as their name, image and likeness,” WME’s digital chief Chris Jacquemin wrote in a memo at the time. “Our position is that artists should have a choice in how they show up in the world and how their likeness is used and we have notified OpenAI that all WME clients be opted out of the latest Sora AI update, regardless of whether IP rights holders have opted out IP our clients are associated with.” With many celebrities, artists, creators and other high-profile figures on Instagram, an opt-out model may not be good enough, especially when their likeness is their livelihood.

sources.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
passages: Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days.
Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks.
You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too.
Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent.

sources.title: I gave Muse access to my emails, credit cards, and health data
passages: If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more?
I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it).
While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me.
A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance.
Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent.
Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction.
Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent.

Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications.

But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue.
I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of.
The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone.
Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet).
"If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through.

extraction.body: There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps. One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

extraction.body: "No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent," the talent agency said in a statement Wednesday night. Meta , led by CEO and AI enthusiast Mark Zuckerberg, this week rolled out the first photo and video tools to come out of its Superintelligence Labs: Muse Photo and Muse Video. The tool brings Meta in line with the state of the art in AI media creation, alongside Google’s Gemini and Seedance 2.0, but along with the tools, Meta also said that all public Instagram profiles will be opt-out, not opt-in, and other users can pull in those other accounts that don’t opt out and create new content using their profiles. For celebrities and other high-profile figures, that could be a major problem, even if most do end up opting out. Now Creative Artists Agency is calling out Meta for the move, and asking the tech giant to make it opt-in, not opt-out. “No one’s name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent. True innovation puts creators first: respecting their rights, protecting their livelihoods, and giving them real control, not handing it over to platforms,” CAA said in a statement Wednesday evening. “We have raised our concerns with Meta on behalf of our clients, voicing our disapproval and perspective on the need for a more responsible approach. We call on Meta to make protection the default on Muse Image, not the exception, and enable individuals to opt-in if they want to allow usage of their image or likeness for AI content creation. “Artists deserve to decide if and how their likeness and work is used, with consent and the ability to set their own terms,” the statement continues. “This means letting creators impose restrictions, monitor usage, and prevent unauthorized endorsements or exploitation. Responsible AI requires clear disclosures and swift removal of unauthorized content. There must be easy ways to spot, track, and take down misuse, and it should be clear when something is AI-generated. CAA believes in the power of new technology, but not at the cost of individuals’ rights or livelihoods. The future of creativity depends on respecting the ownership and autonomy of those who make it possible.” CAA, of course, is well aware of the opportunities and threats posed by generative AI to its clients. The agency maintains what it calls the “CAA Vault,” where the digital likenesses of its clients reside for potential future monetization and protection, and the agency was the first test user of YouTube’s deepfake detection tool, which rolled out to all of Hollywood earlier this year. The Muse situation is reminiscent of the botches launch of OpenAI’s Sora, which was overrun with well-known IP and the likenesses of many high-profile figures, forcing the AI giant to pivot to an opt-in model, before it scrapped the video model altogether earlier this year. After Sora launched, WME said that it was opting out on behalf of all of its clients, the first domino to fall in that model’s short life. “There is a strong need for real protections for artists and creatives as they encounter AI models using their intellectual property, as well as their name, image and likeness,” WME’s digital chief Chris Jacquemin wrote in a memo at the time. “Our position is that artists should have a choice in how they show up in the world and how their likeness is used and we have notified OpenAI that all WME clients be opted out of the latest Sora AI update, regardless of whether IP rights holders have opted out IP our clients are associated with.” With many celebrities, artists, creators and other high-profile figures on Instagram, an opt-out model may not be good enough, especially when their likeness is their livelihood.

At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses.

Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.

sources.title: I gave Muse access to my emails, credit cards, and health data
passages: If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more?
I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it).
While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me.
A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance.
Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent.
Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction.
Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent.

Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications.

But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue.
I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of.
The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone.
Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet).
"If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through.

extraction.body: There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps. One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

The company says this tool allows users to "search the YouTube Music catalog of over 100 million official songs" by using natural sound. All you have to do is tap "search" and look for the waveform icon. Then it's up to you. The tool lets people hum the song, sing the song or even play the song on another instrument. The feature is rolling out to YouTube music subscribers on both iOS and Android. It's also been working on something called AI-generated conversational radio. This isn't a platform in which AI DJs take jobs away from Wolfman Jack or whatever. Rather, it's a tool that lets people use natural conversation to describe the type of radio station they want to listen to. The algorithm will take in that information and create some tailor-made radio. This is sort of like Spotify's AI DJ from a while back , but the conversational element should make the algorithm zero in on your exact tastes as described. The bad news? It's only available to select subscribers at this point, as it's in a testing phase. If successful, it should roll out to more users in the coming months. After all, YouTube first announced the "hum to search" tool in March and its already becoming widely available.

It's also been working on something called AI-generated conversational radio. This isn't a platform in which AI DJs take jobs away from Wolfman Jack or whatever. Rather, it's a tool that lets people use natural conversation to describe the type of radio station they want to listen to. The algorithm will take in that information and create some tailor-made radio. This is sort of like Spotify's AI DJ from a while back , but the conversational element should make the algorithm zero in on your exact tastes as described.

The bad news? It's only available to select subscribers at this point, as it's in a testing phase. If successful, it should roll out to more users in the coming months. After all, YouTube first announced the "hum to search" tool in March and its already becoming widely available.

extraction.body: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss. Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows. Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history. YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation. YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery. The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones. Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes. Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts. The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to. Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide. YouTube announced two AI features for YouTube Music at its Made On YouTube event on 23rd September 2026: Ask Music, a conversational tool for songs and podcasts, and Your Podcast Lineup, a weekly spoken guide to new shows.

Ask Music lives inside the YouTube Music app and takes requests typed the way you’d ask a friend. A listener could request a mix built from the tracks that inspired a song, then ask who played bass on it. YouTube says the tool also lets users customize the queue and “ dive deeper into artist lore. “
The catalog is what makes this interesting. Official studio recordings sit next to covers, live performances, and DJ sets. That gives a chat request far more to pull from than a studio-only library.

YouTube paired the launch with a discovery figure in its announcement : users found an artist new to them over 450 million times in July 2026. Ask Music is built to push that number higher by making the search step conversational.

The idea isn’t entirely new for the app. YouTube Music tested AI music hosts last year that offered stories, fan trivia, and commentary during playback; Ask Music hands that control to the listener instead of scripting it.

YouTube didn’t explain where Ask Music gets its answers on credits and recording history, or how it handles a question it can’t verify. For a tool that tells fans who played on a record, that sourcing will decide how far people trust it.

Your Podcast Lineup goes after a different headache. Most people face more podcasts than they have hours to hear. Even listeners with a settled list of favorites fall behind on new episodes, let alone new shows.

The guide will appear on the podcast page of the YouTube Music app . Each week, it plays a short spoken preview of recommended shows, explains why they might appeal, and then moves straight into suggested episodes. YouTube called the experience “ completely eyes-optional and hands-free. “

Spotify took a different route with its personal podcasts feature, which uses AI to generate episodes from a listener’s interests and prompts. YouTube’s version keeps AI in the narrator’s seat and points listeners to shows that already exist. Human creators stay at the end of the recommendation. It also builds on the AI podcast discovery tools YouTube has already brought to Premium.

For now, the rollout has no date attached. Subscribers who want Your Podcast Lineup should watch the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Whether non-paying listeners get either tool is a question YouTube hasn’t answered.

Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows. Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history. YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation. YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery. The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones. Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes. Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts. The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to. Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide. passages: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight.
Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.

extraction.body: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price. Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content). On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames. Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset. Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets. Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.) Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset. The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras. Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

sources.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
passages: That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them.

The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge.
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses.

Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court.
I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic.
Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too.
I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

extraction.body: Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket. The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged. The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same. [Image: Here’s the compute puck. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands. Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers). Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds. Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

extraction.body: Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses. Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here . Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD. In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°). That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable. Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply. Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical. As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup. Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content. While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S. Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more. Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot. When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand. Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there. At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove , courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies , and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking. Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser. Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio. Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity. The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds. Disclosure: Meta provided lodging for one Road to VR reporter to attend Meta Connect 2026 where information for this article was gathered .

coreStoryFacts.text: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight.
Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device.
It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras.
Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.
A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive.
That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them.

The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge.
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses.

Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court.
I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic.
Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too.
I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

extraction.body: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price. Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content). On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames. Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset. Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets. Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.) Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset. The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras. Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.
