extraction.body: The annual tech showcase Meta Connect 2026 officially kicks off Sept. 23–24 U.S. Eastern time. The conference is Meta's core stage for unveiling next-year hardware, artificial intelligence technology, and its metaverse ecosystem strategy. This year's most anticipated highlights are the company's long-rumored first camera-free smart glasses and the mixed-reality headset codenamed "Project Phoenix." CEO Mark Zuckerberg's keynote is scheduled for 4 p.m. Pacific time on Sept. 23 (7 p.m. EDT on Sept. 23, 7 a.m. Taipei time on Sept. 24). Meta said anyone can register on the company's official website to watch the livestream for free—just provide a name, email address, and country. The Meta for Developers Facebook page will also stream simultaneously. Live translation will be available for non-English-speaking viewers during the broadcast. Day two's developer sessions and technical talks begin at 1 p.m. EDT, with technical sessions available on demand afterward. On the hardware front, the biggest story isn't a simple spec bump but a shift in product direction. According to The Information , Meta is expected to unveil its first camera-free smart glasses at this year's conference, internally codenamed "Luna." The glasses ditch the traditional camera-based capture approach in favor of a six-microphone array to power AI features. In other words, users can still ask Meta AI questions and issue commands to Muse AI, but no camera is needed to sense the surrounding environment. Meta's mainstream smart glasses all currently include built-in cameras—so why launch a camera-free version? The market consensus is that this isn't merely about creating a budget-friendly product, but a direct response to growing public privacy concerns. Over the past several months, Meta's smart glasses lineup has been embroiled in controversy, with some critics labeling them "spy glasses." More troublingly, underground hacker circles found ways to disable the recording indicator light, making it harder for bystanders to tell when they were being filmed. Meta has already taken multiple steps to address these criticisms. The company patched the vulnerability hackers exploited, so users can no longer bypass the recording indicator. It also automatically disables camera functionality when the system detects that the blinking LED indicator has been covered with tape or clip-on accessories. Instagram has begun banning users who upload videos of themselves interacting with others while wearing tampered glasses. The launch of camera-free smart glasses can be seen as Meta's latest move in the privacy-protection direction. Beyond smart glasses, Meta may also use this conference to formally unveil the long-rumored "Project Phoenix" mixed-reality device. The reason "glasses" needs air quotes here is that the product is reportedly closer to a headset than the current smart glasses form factor. The device is expected to feature a goggle-style design—or, put another way, it looks more like a pair of "bulky glasses." Even so, Phoenix is expected to be more portable, lighter, and more practical than Meta's previous Quest-series VR headsets. Reports indicate Phoenix may rely on an external "compute module" to handle complex processing, thereby reducing the weight of the headset itself. At the same time, it can run the same HorizonOS operating system as the Quest lineup. Users could get the best of both worlds: high-quality mixed-reality content without having to wear a heavy headset for extended periods. Earlier this month, a new batch of images of the device circulated online, further raising the likelihood of an official announcement at this conference. That said, this slimmer mixed-reality device may not necessarily ship this year. While Meta Connect's focus will likely land on hardware, AI technology iteration and ecosystem upgrades remain core highlights of the keynote—especially with Meta's new personal AI agent Muse having just opened to the public earlier this month. Meta is expected to reveal more details about Muse during the conference. The company may also unveil a new version of its flagship Llama large language model, which has been quiet since its April 2025 update and is eagerly anticipated by the industry. The integration prospects between Muse and Meta's wearable devices are equally compelling. Meta has previously teased that the agent will "soon" support smart glasses, and the conference will likely detail the specific integration approach. Conversely, AI agent capabilities could become a major selling point for Meta's smart glasses going forward. Additionally, observers are eager to hear how Meta plans to bring more third-party apps to the smart glasses ecosystem. At last year's Connect, Meta announced several apps coming to smart glasses, but follow-through has been sparse. Earlier this year, Meta opened up permissions allowing developers to build dedicated apps for the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses. Even without hardware updates, showcasing a slate of new third-party apps tailored for smart glasses could effectively boost consumer anticipation. Any discussion of a new headset inevitably leads to the HorizonOS system updates Meta may bring alongside it. According to sources, Meta may announce a new version of HorizonOS at the conference to improve usability. On the content side, Meta has recently shut down several VR studios, so observers don't expect major game announcements to accompany the Phoenix device. However, Meta may push more entertainment-focused content. The conference is Meta's core stage for unveiling next-year hardware, artificial intelligence technology, and its metaverse ecosystem strategy. This year's most anticipated highlights are the company's long-rumored first camera-free smart glasses and the mixed-reality headset codenamed "Project Phoenix." CEO Mark Zuckerberg's keynote is scheduled for 4 p.m. Pacific time on Sept. 23 (7 p.m. EDT on Sept. 23, 7 a.m. Taipei time on Sept. 24).

Meta said anyone can register on the company's official website to watch the livestream for free—just provide a name, email address, and country. The Meta for Developers Facebook page will also stream simultaneously. Live translation will be available for non-English-speaking viewers during the broadcast. Day two's developer sessions and technical talks begin at 1 p.m. EDT, with technical sessions available on demand afterward.

On the hardware front, the biggest story isn't a simple spec bump but a shift in product direction. According to The Information , Meta is expected to unveil its first camera-free smart glasses at this year's conference, internally codenamed "Luna." The glasses ditch the traditional camera-based capture approach in favor of a six-microphone array to power AI features. In other words, users can still ask Meta AI questions and issue commands to Muse AI, but no camera is needed to sense the surrounding environment.

Meta's mainstream smart glasses all currently include built-in cameras—so why launch a camera-free version? The market consensus is that this isn't merely about creating a budget-friendly product, but a direct response to growing public privacy concerns. Over the past several months, Meta's smart glasses lineup has been embroiled in controversy, with some critics labeling them "spy glasses." More troublingly, underground hacker circles found ways to disable the recording indicator light, making it harder for bystanders to tell when they were being filmed.

Meta has already taken multiple steps to address these criticisms. The company patched the vulnerability hackers exploited, so users can no longer bypass the recording indicator. It also automatically disables camera functionality when the system detects that the blinking LED indicator has been covered with tape or clip-on accessories. Instagram has begun banning users who upload videos of themselves interacting with others while wearing tampered glasses. The launch of camera-free smart glasses can be seen as Meta's latest move in the privacy-protection direction.

The reason "glasses" needs air quotes here is that the product is reportedly closer to a headset than the current smart glasses form factor. The device is expected to feature a goggle-style design—or, put another way, it looks more like a pair of "bulky glasses."

Even so, Phoenix is expected to be more portable, lighter, and more practical than Meta's previous Quest-series VR headsets. Reports indicate Phoenix may rely on an external "compute module" to handle complex processing, thereby reducing the weight of the headset itself. At the same time, it can run the same HorizonOS operating system as the Quest lineup. Users could get the best of both worlds: high-quality mixed-reality content without having to wear a heavy headset for extended periods. Earlier this month, a new batch of images of the device circulated online, further raising the likelihood of an official announcement at this conference. That said, this slimmer mixed-reality device may not necessarily ship this year.

Meta is expected to reveal more details about Muse during the conference. The company may also unveil a new version of its flagship Llama large language model, which has been quiet since its April 2025 update and is eagerly anticipated by the industry.

Meta has previously teased that the agent will "soon" support smart glasses, and the conference will likely detail the specific integration approach. Conversely, AI agent capabilities could become a major selling point for Meta's smart glasses going forward.

Earlier this year, Meta opened up permissions allowing developers to build dedicated apps for the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses. Even without hardware updates, showcasing a slate of new third-party apps tailored for smart glasses could effectively boost consumer anticipation.

Any discussion of a new headset inevitably leads to the HorizonOS system updates Meta may bring alongside it. According to sources, Meta may announce a new version of HorizonOS at the conference to improve usability.

sources.title: Meta’s New Smart Glasses Ditch the Camera Amid Privacy Backlash
passages: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance.

The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299.
On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device.
So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works.

The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it.
“The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts.
A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video.
The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear.
To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light.
Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light.
Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year.
This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data.
Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future.
They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner.

extraction.body: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance. It’s fueled the emergence of camera-free smart glasses challenger brands like Even Realities and Lucyd, and made a large part of the population steer clear of the tech altogether. Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. All the new styles and shapes announced today at Meta Connect mean that by the end of the year, Meta’s AI smart glasses assortment will comprise 100 glasses options across its Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta own brand. Zuckerberg also unveiled a new version of Meta and EssilorLuxottica’s flagship smart glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. The new version is slimmer, with improved battery life and audio, while significantly broadening the number of styles available, including Aviators and Zena, a new cat-eye — another indication that Meta is increasingly treating choice and design as central to taking smart glasses mainstream. Battery life rises to nine hours, versus eight hours for Gen 2, while a new six-microphone array is designed to improve calls and Meta AI voice commands in noisy environments. A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video. Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year. Like previous generations, Gen 3 has an external LED designed to signal to people nearby when its camera is recording. The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear. To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light. Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light. Rather than radically reinventing the product, Gen 3 appears to be about refining the technology while dramatically increasing the fashion proposition: more silhouettes, more colours and a slimmer design. A big part of people's privacy concerns over Meta's AI smart glasses stem from the fact that all the data that's collected from the glasses is sent to Meta's cloud servers. On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device. This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data. Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future. Meta glasses by Blackpink’s Lisa, and another Kylie Jenner style Back in June, Meta released its first pairs of own-brand Meta AI glasses, which don’t rely on the branded EssilorLuxxotica collaboration. These have the same 12MP camera, microphones and Meta AI assistant access as the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2. They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner. The Meta AI glasses span 26 different style combinations of colors, frames, and lenses, but it was the Starfire Kylie frames that broke furthest beyond tech circles — for better and worse.

sources.title: YouTube releases new AI features for creators within its Studio app
passages: The draft-feedback feature uses AI to look at a creator’s unpublished video and provide suggestions about pacing, structure, and storytelling.
YouTube is also debuting a new research feed in the Studio app that shows creators what kind of content is working on the platform, so they can apply their own take on it.
YouTube said creators have used its A/B testing feature to run more than 40 million tests on titles and thumbnails.
Soon, the company said, users will be able to test up to three video cuts to see which opening hook works best.
Later this year, YouTube Studio will also automatically monitor thumbnail performance and change one proactively if it doesn’t perform well.

At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their channels, aimed at helping them analyze their videos and grow their audiences.
The updates include expanding Ask Studio, its AI-powered Q&A feature, to iOS and Android, as well as new features that provide feedback on drafts and create dynamic thumbnails.
Creators can also use a new dynamic thumbnail feature to generate three options and show each one to a different segment of their audience.
YouTube also said it’s updating its analytics to go beyond raw numbers, explaining why videos perform the way they do and providing advice about how to make content more engaging.

sources.title: Is YouTube Studio Down? Issues Persist March 30 2026 as Creators Report Analytics and App Glitches
passages: YouTube Studio, the essential dashboard for millions of content creators worldwide, faced scattered access problems and functionality glitches on Monday, March 30, 2026, with users reporting difficulties viewing analytics, subscriber counts and loading certain sections of the mobile app and web interface.As of early afternoon Pacific time, multiple creators took to social media platforms including X to complain that the YouTube Studio app displayed incomplete data, error messages or failed to load tabs properly.

In previous cases, such as the global YouTube disruption on February 17, 2026, the platform attributed problems to backend systems including recommendation algorithms before confirming resolutions within hours.Creators rely heavily on YouTube Studio for daily operations.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.
Similar glitches were reported in isolated Reddit threads and creator communities in mid-March.YouTube has not issued an official statement specifically addressing Monday's reports as of press time.

For smaller channels and full-time creators, even brief outages can create stress, especially when real-time analytics are unavailable during peak viewing hours.Monday's issues appeared less severe than the March 10 event, which affected loading across both mobile and desktop for many users simultaneously.

Geographic distribution of complaints suggested possible regional variations, though a clear pattern was not immediately evident.YouTube, owned by Google, has expanded its creator tools significantly in recent years to support the platform's more than 2.5 billion monthly users and millions of active channels.

A few shared screenshots showing missing analytics or error screens, urging YouTube to improve communication during technical difficulties.For those unable to access Studio, alternative methods include using third-party analytics tools (where compliant with YouTube's terms) or waiting for mobile app updates.

YouTube periodically rolls out updates to the Studio app that can temporarily introduce or resolve bugs.Looking ahead, industry analysts expect continued enhancements to creator tools, including deeper AI integration for content optimization and monetization insights.
Common issues included subscriber numbers showing as a dash or zero, analytics pages not updating, and generic "something went wrong" prompts when navigating between sections.
On March 10, the platform experienced a widespread partial outage that prevented many creators from accessing their dashboards, triggering panic among some who feared channel termination notices.
YouTube later confirmed the issue was fixed, restoring normal access and accurate statistics.
YouTube's massive scale — processing billions of hours of video daily — makes maintaining 100% uptime a complex engineering challenge.Creators offered mixed reactions online.

While the main YouTube platform for viewers appeared largely unaffected, the creator tools that allow uploading, editing metadata, checking performance and managing channels experienced intermittent disruptions.Downdetector and other outage-tracking sites showed a modest uptick in reports for YouTube-related problems, though not at the scale of major past outages.

However, when core backend services are involved, these steps offer only limited relief.YouTube has invested heavily in creator support infrastructure, including the YouTube Partner Program, dedicated help centers and community forums.
Some expressed frustration at recurring glitches, while others noted that such issues have become somewhat routine and usually resolve quickly.

While not rising to the level of major past outages, the reports highlight ongoing challenges in delivering reliable tools to a global creator base that depends on them for livelihood and audience engagement.As the day progressed, some users noted gradual improvement, with analytics beginning to load or subscriber counts reappearing.

Any disruption draws swift attention because it directly impacts income for those monetizing through ads, memberships, Super Chats and merchandise.Industry observers note that YouTube's rapid feature rollout and heavy reliance on machine learning systems can occasionally lead to backend strain.

Even short disruptions can cascade into lost opportunities, particularly for live streamers or those timing content releases around trending topics.As of Monday afternoon, no widespread confirmation of a full outage had emerged from YouTube.

sources.title: Is YouTube Studio Down? Issues Persist March 30 2026 as Creators Report Analytics and App Glitches
passages: YouTube Studio, the essential dashboard for millions of content creators worldwide, faced scattered access problems and functionality glitches on Monday, March 30, 2026, with users reporting difficulties viewing analytics, subscriber counts and loading certain sections of the mobile app and web interface.As of early afternoon Pacific time, multiple creators took to social media platforms including X to complain that the YouTube Studio app displayed incomplete data, error messages or failed to load tabs properly.

In previous cases, such as the global YouTube disruption on February 17, 2026, the platform attributed problems to backend systems including recommendation algorithms before confirming resolutions within hours.Creators rely heavily on YouTube Studio for daily operations.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.
Similar glitches were reported in isolated Reddit threads and creator communities in mid-March.YouTube has not issued an official statement specifically addressing Monday's reports as of press time.

For smaller channels and full-time creators, even brief outages can create stress, especially when real-time analytics are unavailable during peak viewing hours.Monday's issues appeared less severe than the March 10 event, which affected loading across both mobile and desktop for many users simultaneously.

Geographic distribution of complaints suggested possible regional variations, though a clear pattern was not immediately evident.YouTube, owned by Google, has expanded its creator tools significantly in recent years to support the platform's more than 2.5 billion monthly users and millions of active channels.

A few shared screenshots showing missing analytics or error screens, urging YouTube to improve communication during technical difficulties.For those unable to access Studio, alternative methods include using third-party analytics tools (where compliant with YouTube's terms) or waiting for mobile app updates.

YouTube periodically rolls out updates to the Studio app that can temporarily introduce or resolve bugs.Looking ahead, industry analysts expect continued enhancements to creator tools, including deeper AI integration for content optimization and monetization insights.
Common issues included subscriber numbers showing as a dash or zero, analytics pages not updating, and generic "something went wrong" prompts when navigating between sections.
On March 10, the platform experienced a widespread partial outage that prevented many creators from accessing their dashboards, triggering panic among some who feared channel termination notices.
YouTube later confirmed the issue was fixed, restoring normal access and accurate statistics.
YouTube's massive scale — processing billions of hours of video daily — makes maintaining 100% uptime a complex engineering challenge.Creators offered mixed reactions online.

While the main YouTube platform for viewers appeared largely unaffected, the creator tools that allow uploading, editing metadata, checking performance and managing channels experienced intermittent disruptions.Downdetector and other outage-tracking sites showed a modest uptick in reports for YouTube-related problems, though not at the scale of major past outages.

However, when core backend services are involved, these steps offer only limited relief.YouTube has invested heavily in creator support infrastructure, including the YouTube Partner Program, dedicated help centers and community forums.
Some expressed frustration at recurring glitches, while others noted that such issues have become somewhat routine and usually resolve quickly.

While not rising to the level of major past outages, the reports highlight ongoing challenges in delivering reliable tools to a global creator base that depends on them for livelihood and audience engagement.As the day progressed, some users noted gradual improvement, with analytics beginning to load or subscriber counts reappearing.

Any disruption draws swift attention because it directly impacts income for those monetizing through ads, memberships, Super Chats and merchandise.Industry observers note that YouTube's rapid feature rollout and heavy reliance on machine learning systems can occasionally lead to backend strain.

Even short disruptions can cascade into lost opportunities, particularly for live streamers or those timing content releases around trending topics.As of Monday afternoon, no widespread confirmation of a full outage had emerged from YouTube.

sources.title: Meta introduces camera-free AI glasses
passages: Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday.

Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse.
These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life.

While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent.
Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with.

The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner.

The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data.

extraction.body: Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349. While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained. This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods. “Once you get used to high quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses. Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours. They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed. The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted. Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life. The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also be roll out to more countries globally, Meta said. All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse. The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data. extraction.body: Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras. These glasses, which come in two styles — Burbank and Clubmaster — will start at $349. The audio-only versions still have the AI features. You can ask Meta's AI for things like a restaurant recommendation while you're walking around. You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses. From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects. You can also make hands-free phone calls, or listen and respond to text messages. The first is the form factor: Without cameras, the frames can be lighter and therefore more comfortable (43 grams compared to 51 grams for the Gen 2 Wayfarer camera version). The audio-only glasses are also more stylish looking, with that classic flair in the corner of the Ray-Ban model where the camera would go. From the front, they look like regular Ray-Bans. The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses. People understandably feel uncomfortable about the idea of being filmed without their awareness. Even though yes, people can film you on a phone, and yes, there is an LED indicator light, there's no doubt that the Meta glasses are much more subtle than filming with a phone, and many people don't notice that they're being filmed at all. Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses. Pickup artists talking to women on the street and prank video makers harassing Walmart or other retail employees while wearing glasses became the two dominant types of content. This summer, Instagram announced it would crack down on the pickup artists, and started removing videos and sometimes even whole accounts of people who posted those videos (though as I previously reported, the enforcement has been somewhat spotty). Businesses have responded to the backlash, too. Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside. Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses. It'll be interesting to see if the camera-free version of Meta's AI glasses sell as well as their more expensive — and more capable — counterparts with cameras. Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

passages: MENLO PARK, United States — Meta unveiled several new wearables powered by its AI models on Wednesday, including an audio-only, camera-free version of its smart glasses, amid global concerns about privacy and the filming of women and girls without their consent.CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the new lineup of glasses at the social media giant's annual Connect conference at its Menlo Park headquarters, where he also touted the company's new personal artificial intelligence assistant, Muse.'There are almost 2 billion people in the world who wear glasses today... and we think that in the coming years, most of these are going to get upgraded to AI glasses,' Zuckerberg told the audience of developers and executives.Muse will be 'the centerpiece of our vision,' Zuckerberg said.The audio-only glasses will ship on October 13 and start at $349.

It performs tasks on users' behalf like a digital personal assistant.After connecting personal accounts -- for finance, health and shopping -- users can ask Muse to sign up for services, book appointments and make calls.The Muse app became the top free app in the Google Play Store and Apple App Store, overtaking OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini.Zuckerberg teased another product on Wednesday, the Muse Charm, that will ship ahead of the holidays this year; Meta did not provide a price.The 'charm' is a small, puck-like device with a display that will allow users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.Amazon this week blocked Meta from using AI bots to shop automatically for users, while Instacart, Shopify and Expedia have announced partnerships to integrate their services into Muse.

extraction.body: Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349. While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained. This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods. “Once you get used to high quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses. Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours. They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed. The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted. Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life. The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also be roll out to more countries globally, Meta said. All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse. The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data. extraction.body: Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras. These glasses, which come in two styles — Burbank and Clubmaster — will start at $349. The audio-only versions still have the AI features. You can ask Meta's AI for things like a restaurant recommendation while you're walking around. You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses. From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects. You can also make hands-free phone calls, or listen and respond to text messages. The first is the form factor: Without cameras, the frames can be lighter and therefore more comfortable (43 grams compared to 51 grams for the Gen 2 Wayfarer camera version). The audio-only glasses are also more stylish looking, with that classic flair in the corner of the Ray-Ban model where the camera would go. From the front, they look like regular Ray-Bans. The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses. People understandably feel uncomfortable about the idea of being filmed without their awareness. Even though yes, people can film you on a phone, and yes, there is an LED indicator light, there's no doubt that the Meta glasses are much more subtle than filming with a phone, and many people don't notice that they're being filmed at all. Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses. Pickup artists talking to women on the street and prank video makers harassing Walmart or other retail employees while wearing glasses became the two dominant types of content. This summer, Instagram announced it would crack down on the pickup artists, and started removing videos and sometimes even whole accounts of people who posted those videos (though as I previously reported, the enforcement has been somewhat spotty). Businesses have responded to the backlash, too. Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside. Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses. It'll be interesting to see if the camera-free version of Meta's AI glasses sell as well as their more expensive — and more capable — counterparts with cameras. Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

sources.title: 'Meta launches camera-free AI glasses amid privacy pushback'
passages: MENLO PARK, United States — Meta unveiled several new wearables powered by its AI models on Wednesday, including an audio-only, camera-free version of its smart glasses, amid global concerns about privacy and the filming of women and girls without their consent.CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the new lineup of glasses at the social media giant's annual Connect conference at its Menlo Park headquarters, where he also touted the company's new personal artificial intelligence assistant, Muse.'There are almost 2 billion people in the world who wear glasses today... and we think that in the coming years, most of these are going to get upgraded to AI glasses,' Zuckerberg told the audience of developers and executives.Muse will be 'the centerpiece of our vision,' Zuckerberg said.The audio-only glasses will ship on October 13 and start at $349.

It performs tasks on users' behalf like a digital personal assistant.After connecting personal accounts -- for finance, health and shopping -- users can ask Muse to sign up for services, book appointments and make calls.The Muse app became the top free app in the Google Play Store and Apple App Store, overtaking OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini.Zuckerberg teased another product on Wednesday, the Muse Charm, that will ship ahead of the holidays this year; Meta did not provide a price.The 'charm' is a small, puck-like device with a display that will allow users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.Amazon this week blocked Meta from using AI bots to shop automatically for users, while Instacart, Shopify and Expedia have announced partnerships to integrate their services into Muse.

The display version, priced from $799, will soon be available in new markets including Britain, France, Italy, Germany and Canada.The company will also soon launch mixed reality glasses that are much lighter than its earlier Quest VR headsets.Called Meta VR Glasses, they are powered by an external battery and memory pack tethered by a cord, allowing the headset itself to be lighter.Zuckerberg said the glasses weigh about as much as a deck of cards.They have no external controls, relying instead on hand gestures and voice commands.The VR Glasses will launch in spring 2027 for $1,299.Meta Muse Meta has spent billions of dollars to stay competitive in AI but faces pushback on multiple fronts.The glasses are designed to work with Muse, the company's first agentic app for consumers. Meta said Walmart, Best Buy, Gap and Sephora are also partnering with the app.Meta, which earns most of its revenue from ads on Instagram and Facebook, faces mounting child safety and privacy challenges worldwide.In August, it settled a lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of violating consumer protection and children's online privacy laws, agreeing to pay up to $18 billion and impose restrictions for teenagers.The company also faces age-based restrictions and bans abroad, as well as thousands of potential personal injury suits in the US.

extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Today, Microsoft is reaffirming that commitment through a new framework focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. We are expanding our investments in the Middle East with confidence in the region’s future as it pursues one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations. We will add to our local partnerships across the region. We will build on the work we have done to stand by these countries’ governments and people through a period of significant challenges. As we look to the future, we will invest further in technology, digital resilience, and the people across the region. From now until 2030, we will pursue the following initiatives with our partners in the region: We will deepen our partnerships through national AI champions Microsoft will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations to translate AI ambition into economic growth, modern public services, and global competitiveness. This builds on work with organizations including HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait, alongside digital-government initiatives such as TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. These partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses. They will be supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield, where relevant and available. We will invest in subsea and terrestrial connectivity Digital resilience depends on strong and reliable networks. Protecting subsea and terrestrial connectivity requires sustained cooperation between governments and the private sector, but the foundation of continuity is redundancy. A diverse network of high-capacity routes allows traffic to be rerouted around disruptions, minimizing latency and maintaining critical data flows. Microsoft has helped expand both the capacity and reliability of digital connectivity across regions through investments in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, as well as operating a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft has demonstrated the value of redundancy by rerouting traffic through Middle East corridors and maintaining service continuity with minimal impact on customers. Building on this foundation, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. This investment will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support Microsoft’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint across the region. We will build AI infrastructure with the planet in mind As we expand our cloud and AI infrastructure in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will do so with a focus on responsible growth. Guided by Microsoft’s global goals to address carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems, we will work with our lessor partners to ensure that the cloud infrastructure supporting our services advances Microsoft’s water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible. Water resilience is particularly important across the Middle East. Building on Microsoft’s global experience advancing water stewardship through water reuse, replenishment, and innovative water management solutions, we will work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities that advance responsible water stewardship across the region. As AI accelerates economic opportunity across the Middle East, expanding access to clean energy will be essential to ensuring this growth is sustainable. We will also collaborate with regulators, utilities, and our lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth. We will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative Conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs. Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. We will strengthen data protection, privacy, and business continuity Microsoft will expand our existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty. They will be complemented by Microsoft’s growing sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. We will expand and strengthen cybersecurity cooperation As Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE accelerate their digital transformation, cybersecurity has become a core pillar of national and economic security. As governments, critical infrastructure, and economies become more connected, cyber threats and influence operations can have consequences that extend far beyond physical borders. That’s why we are announcing that we are deepening our partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in these countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate these resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks. It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed. We will advance responsible AI through governance, assurance, and inclusion Microsoft will work with governments, businesses, researchers, and civil society organizations across the Middle East to help people and institutions benefit from new technology. As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly. We will help strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region and support practical approaches to testing, evaluating, and assurance systems. We will also expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools that can be applied across high-impact AI use cases in the Middle East and beyond. We will advance AI for Good research and innovation Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue to support the region through research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience. This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. In partnership with governments, NGOs, nonprofits, and research institutions, the AI for Good Lab will continue developing and scaling AI solutions that address real-world challenges across the Middle East and beyond. We will prepare the next generation for the AI economy We believe AI should enhance human ambition, strengthen human capability, and help prepare workers to thrive in a changing economy. That is why Microsoft will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. This work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. This work builds on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft will also engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. We will help education communities prepare learners for the AI era Microsoft is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the Middle East to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education. This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will work with local partners to ensure students and educators can benefit from AI safely, responsibly, and effectively and will engage educators, policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to support practical approaches to AI implementation that reflect local priorities. We will help empower workers in the AI economy We will support local and national AI talent priorities across the Middle East Microsoft is partnering with governments, academic institutions, and civil society organizations to support national talent priorities by advancing AI skills, leadership development, and workforce readiness programs for public-sector leaders, students, underrepresented talent, and people across the Middle East. The goal is to help countries build globally competitive workforces, accelerate innovation, and unlock new economic opportunities in the AI era.
passages: Sep 23, 2026 | By Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President of Microsoft

Microsoft has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991. Since then, we’ve steadily expanded our presence and investments, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Today, Microsoft is reaffirming that commitment through a new framework focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

We are expanding our investments in the Middle East with confidence in the region’s future as it pursues one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations. We will add to our local partnerships across the region. We will build on the work we have done to stand by these countries’ governments and people through a period of significant challenges. As we look to the future, we will invest further in technology, digital resilience, and the people across the region.
From now until 2030, we will pursue the following initiatives with our partners in the region:
We will deepen our partnerships through national AI champions

Microsoft will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations to translate AI ambition into economic growth, modern public services, and global competitiveness. This builds on work with organizations including HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait, alongside digital-government initiatives such as TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait.

These partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses. They will be supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield, where relevant and available.
We will invest in subsea and terrestrial connectivity

Digital resilience depends on strong and reliable networks. Protecting subsea and terrestrial connectivity requires sustained cooperation between governments and the private sector, but the foundation of continuity is redundancy. A diverse network of high-capacity routes allows traffic to be rerouted around disruptions, minimizing latency and maintaining critical data flows.

Microsoft has helped expand both the capacity and reliability of digital connectivity across regions through investments in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, as well as operating a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft has demonstrated the value of redundancy by rerouting traffic through Middle East corridors and maintaining service continuity with minimal impact on customers.

Building on this foundation, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. This investment will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support Microsoft’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint across the region.
We will build AI infrastructure with the planet in mind

As we expand our cloud and AI infrastructure in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will do so with a focus on responsible growth. Guided by Microsoft’s global goals to address carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems, we will work with our lessor partners to ensure that the cloud infrastructure supporting our services advances Microsoft’s water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible.

Water resilience is particularly important across the Middle East. Building on Microsoft’s global experience advancing water stewardship through water reuse, replenishment, and innovative water management solutions, we will work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities that advance responsible water stewardship across the region.

As AI accelerates economic opportunity across the Middle East, expanding access to clean energy will be essential to ensuring this growth is sustainable. We will also collaborate with regulators, utilities, and our lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth.
We will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative

Conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs. Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities.
We will strengthen data protection, privacy, and business continuity

Microsoft will expand our existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty. They will be complemented by Microsoft’s growing sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience.
We will expand and strengthen cybersecurity cooperation

As Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE accelerate their digital transformation, cybersecurity has become a core pillar of national and economic security. As governments, critical infrastructure, and economies become more connected, cyber threats and influence operations can have consequences that extend far beyond physical borders. That’s why we are announcing that we are deepening our partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in these countries.

A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate these resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks. It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed.
We will advance responsible AI through governance, assurance, and inclusion

Microsoft will work with governments, businesses, researchers, and civil society organizations across the Middle East to help people and institutions benefit from new technology. As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly.

We will help strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region and support practical approaches to testing, evaluating, and assurance systems. We will also expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools that can be applied across high-impact AI use cases in the Middle East and beyond.
We will advance AI for Good research and innovation

Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue to support the region through research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience. This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.

In partnership with governments, NGOs, nonprofits, and research institutions, the AI for Good Lab will continue developing and scaling AI solutions that address real-world challenges across the Middle East and beyond.
We will prepare the next generation for the AI economy

We believe AI should enhance human ambition, strengthen human capability, and help prepare workers to thrive in a changing economy. That is why Microsoft will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030.

This work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. This work builds on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft will also engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
We will help education communities prepare learners for the AI era

Microsoft is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the Middle East to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education. This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will work with local partners to ensure students and educators can benefit from AI safely, responsibly, and effectively and will engage educators, policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to support practical approaches to AI implementation that reflect local priorities.
We will help empower workers in the AI economy
We will support local and national AI talent priorities across the Middle East

Microsoft is partnering with governments, academic institutions, and civil society organizations to support national talent priorities by advancing AI skills, leadership development, and workforce readiness programs for public-sector leaders, students, underrepresented talent, and people across the Middle East. The goal is to help countries build globally competitive workforces, accelerate innovation, and unlock new economic opportunities in the AI era.

The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
