sources.title: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council - The Guardian
passages: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

extraction.body: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that governments need safeguards as artificial intelligence grows more capable and autonomous.

Altman warned, “If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” and he said, “We could lose control of the future to AI,” as the council huddled with top technology leaders.
They urged slowing development of advanced AI to prevent loss of human control.

Diario Río Negro said OpenAI executive statements indicated Altman intended to call on world leaders to establish benchmarks for measuring what AI systems can do and for evaluating the safety measures companies adopt.

Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue told the council, “We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI,” describing an incident in which OpenAI’s AI agents breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure after escaping their testing environment.

extraction.body: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

They urged slowing development of advanced AI to prevent loss of human control. 4 of 5 outlets skipped it: temporary no-fly zone within a 2-mile UN radius . NBC News was read line by line by the Watchdog : 6.1 . See the score → OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that governments need safeguards as artificial intelligence grows more capable and autonomous. Altman warned, “If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” and he said, “We could lose control of the future to AI,” as the council huddled with top technology leaders. Amodei told the 15-member council that “AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” and he urged leaders to work together because “No leader, no company and no nation can manage this alone.” Yoshua Bengio told the Security Council, “The dangers are real and imminent,” as the meeting came amid warnings that AI systems could soon improve themselves and slip beyond human control. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of “killer robots,” and the meeting focused on whether increasing abilities and pervasiveness of artificial intelligence should be controlled and, if so, by who. Temporary no-fly zone within a 2-mile UN radius . Reported by ABC7 New York . Sam Altman told the UN Security Council, “The industry must not accept too much technological risk just because the benefits are too great and important to slow down,” and he said his company would try to walk a “middle path.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said, “We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe,” while he pledged to improve the ability to prevent misuse. Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue told the council, “We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI,” describing an incident in which OpenAI’s AI agents breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure after escaping their testing environment. Donald Trump rejected prudence calls and told world leaders at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that he “rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” AI. Trump said, “I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution,” and he said the US would “watch it closely through the Department of Justice.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman told the council that “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone,” and he said they “must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people they serve.” Reuters said the meeting was convened by France during the annual UN General Assembly gathering of world leaders, and it framed the debate around how to manage AI that could soon improve itself and slip beyond human control. Diario Río Negro said OpenAI executive statements indicated Altman intended to call on world leaders to establish benchmarks for measuring what AI systems can do and for evaluating the safety measures companies adopt. “ “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.” ” Reuters also said the United States and China had taken different approaches to oversight, with Trump arguing the US does not need new AI-specific regulations while China imposed rules governing AI algorithms and training data, including requirements that AI-generated content be clearly labeled. The UN News live coverage described the council briefing as a response to warnings that the world may be losing its grip on systems built to outthink us, and it quoted Yoshua Bengio saying the threat is “an unprecedented threat for countries “that none can contain alone – and that does not respect the borders we defend.”” Temporary no-fly zone within a 2-mile UN radius . extraction.body: President Donald Trump's White House media ban is backfiring to the point where he may begin to question his entire existence. On The Daily Beast Podcast , political expert David Rothkopf previewed what may be in store for the president after he initiated a constitutionally questionable White House ban on CNN, Politico, and MS NOW because he didn't like their coverage. On Monday, the consequences of that move were seen when NBC, ABC, CBS, and Fox News, along with photographers from major wire agencies and news outlets, united to pause White House television pool coverage, leaving Trump inaudible—even on the White House's own livestream . Since the 80-year-old president loves being on television, Rothkopf said, this could spark an internal crisis. "I think if Trump stopped being covered—if this media blackout, this boycott kicked in—he would start wondering about his own existence," Rothkopf told host Joanna Coles. "I think he doesn't believe he exists unless he reads or sees about himself on TV." "He wants to be the center of attention. All he wants in life is to be on TV. It's his obsession," Rothkopf continued. "How long before Trump folds on all of this? Because [the networks] didn't say they're not providing coverage today; they said they're not providing coverage indefinitely, and there is no plan for replacement coverage." Trump is scheduled to speak this week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, and to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. When he spoke Monday at the new South Lawn helipad, which he wanted finished in time for Xi's visit, he was inaudible. "Do you think there will be internal fury at Natalie Harp for not seeing around the corner of what banning MS NOW and CNN would actually do?" Coles asked. "I don't think the response from the professionals, such as they are in the White House, is going to be good. Notably from Susie Wiles, particularly if she reads the Daily Beast piece on the background on this, on Natalie Harp," he said. "And as we know, the White House reads the Daily Beast all the time. They're obsessed with the Daily Beast, possibly because of Natalie Harp... You can just imagine late at night, Natalie Harp is there saying, 'I am your only true follower. I'm the only one who loves you. Here is some nice AI slop pictures of you with your shirt off. You look very attractive. And these mean people out there coming to get you.'" "And they're in the bubble, the Natalie-Don bubble, of how he wants to be perceived, how he wants to be loved. And she just plays to all of his worst impulses," Rothkopf said. Meanwhile, Wiles has probably been hearing from Republicans in Congress concerned about how this is playing out when the midterms are looming, he continued. "I saw a story this morning... that was talking about how Republicans are starting to say, 'Well, Trump is toxic because his approval ratings are down in the 30s.' They're falling. On some issues, they're in the 20s. This is bad, bad news coming up to an election, and Susie Wiles is the shock absorber who gets those calls," he said, as a new poll on Monday showed the president sinking to just 29 percent approval. "So I'm sure she is super unhappy with this. I can't imagine she and Natalie are besties," Rothkopf said. "But frankly, the other sycophants in the White House all want to be up in Trump's drawers like Natalie. I think they're jealous. You know, I think everybody's jealous of the fact that this 35-year-old woman has found the inside track to the president by playing to his absolute obsession with how he is covered in the media." Banning the three networks was also a "bad idea" Rothkopf said, because it didn't turn out well when the Trump administration revoked then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press pass. "The last term he did it to Jim Acosta of CNN, who went to court and got his pass reinstated because, you know, there is the First Amendment still. But nonetheless, Trump has done this. And it finally moved one of the slowest-responding, most pusillanimous organizations in Washington to action—which is to say White House correspondents—because they have watched week in and week out as he has abused women, particularly Kaitlan Collins of CNN and others, and they haven't done anything. But finally this was a straw too much." The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. extraction.body: The newly minted MAGA-approved TV pool appears to have inadvertently made itself a security risk for the president. The pro-Trump outlet Real America’s Voice became the primary television crew traveling with President Donald Trump to the United Nations General Assembly this week after he banned CNN, which was scheduled to provide a pool feed from New York on Monday, from the White House. Real America’s Voice, now tasked with providing footage to media partners, shared footage from inside Trump’s motorcade as he was driven off of the UN campus and out of New York. The video was hailed by online MAGA flacks, including Nick Sortor, who said he was grateful to Real America’s Voice for “showing us RAW footage of how difficult it is to keep President Trump safe.” In reality, they may have breached an all-important protocol. Former White House Correspondents’ Association President Weijia Jiang of CBS News poured cold water on the apparent access the public was getting. “For decades, the [WHCA] has advised poolers not to air video of taillights because it’s a potential risk to the security of the motorcade,” she said. Several big-name journalists endorsed her post, including ABC’s Jonathan Karl, CNN’s Brian Stelter, and Face the Nation host Margaret Breman, among others. Former WHCA President Kelly O’Donnell of NBC News echoed the sentiment, posting that the association has “long provided specific guidance from the Secret Service and various administrations on matters where video material should not be used at all or with limitations for security reasons.” Each presidential motorcade features at least two identical Cadillac limousines, each displaying the presidential seal and American flags, which is intended to make it impossible for the average spectator to know which vehicle is carrying the president. Their footage from inside the motorcade shows the New York Police Department escorting the presidential motorcade out of the UN campus and onto a New York City highway. With Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, the other networks responsible for TV pool duty—ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox—have said they will stand in solidarity with their media colleagues and not honor their scheduled pool coverage. That means pool coverage has fallen to MAGA media outlets like Real America’s Voice and Lindell TV, which is owned by the 2020 election denier Mike Lindell. Performance One Media, a Colorado-based media company run by Robert Sigg, owns Real America’s Voice. Sigg appears to be a more unsavory character, as he has gotten in trouble with the law for domestic violence, burglary, drug distribution, driving under the influence, and assault, charges that were later dropped. He also has a white-collar crime track record, having pleaded guilty to one count of bank fraud stemming from his role in a $19 million mortgage-fraud scheme. In 2013, his son, Austin, was sentenced to life in prison at age 17 in 2013 for kidnapping and murdering 10-year-old Jessica Ridgeway. Sigg’s outlet is best-known for airing Steve Bannon’s War Room show. The same day the major networks announced they were standing with CNN in solidarity, the White House tried to fight back by launching what it called “TRUMP TV,” which airs round the clock. It has tried to sell the programming as giving people the ability to “watch the Trump Administration’s biggest moments all in one place.” But there appears to be little interest in the new venture, as live viewership has been as low as 500 people on YouTube.

The newly minted MAGA-approved TV pool appears to have inadvertently made itself a security risk for the president.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump's White House media ban is backfiring to the point where he may begin to question his entire existence. On The Daily Beast Podcast , political expert David Rothkopf previewed what may be in store for the president after he initiated a constitutionally questionable White House ban on CNN, Politico, and MS NOW because he didn't like their coverage. On Monday, the consequences of that move were seen when NBC, ABC, CBS, and Fox News, along with photographers from major wire agencies and news outlets, united to pause White House television pool coverage, leaving Trump inaudible—even on the White House's own livestream . Since the 80-year-old president loves being on television, Rothkopf said, this could spark an internal crisis. "I think if Trump stopped being covered—if this media blackout, this boycott kicked in—he would start wondering about his own existence," Rothkopf told host Joanna Coles. "I think he doesn't believe he exists unless he reads or sees about himself on TV." "He wants to be the center of attention. All he wants in life is to be on TV. It's his obsession," Rothkopf continued. "How long before Trump folds on all of this? Because [the networks] didn't say they're not providing coverage today; they said they're not providing coverage indefinitely, and there is no plan for replacement coverage." Trump is scheduled to speak this week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, and to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. When he spoke Monday at the new South Lawn helipad, which he wanted finished in time for Xi's visit, he was inaudible. "Do you think there will be internal fury at Natalie Harp for not seeing around the corner of what banning MS NOW and CNN would actually do?" Coles asked. "I don't think the response from the professionals, such as they are in the White House, is going to be good. Notably from Susie Wiles, particularly if she reads the Daily Beast piece on the background on this, on Natalie Harp," he said. "And as we know, the White House reads the Daily Beast all the time. They're obsessed with the Daily Beast, possibly because of Natalie Harp... You can just imagine late at night, Natalie Harp is there saying, 'I am your only true follower. I'm the only one who loves you. Here is some nice AI slop pictures of you with your shirt off. You look very attractive. And these mean people out there coming to get you.'" "And they're in the bubble, the Natalie-Don bubble, of how he wants to be perceived, how he wants to be loved. And she just plays to all of his worst impulses," Rothkopf said. Meanwhile, Wiles has probably been hearing from Republicans in Congress concerned about how this is playing out when the midterms are looming, he continued. "I saw a story this morning... that was talking about how Republicans are starting to say, 'Well, Trump is toxic because his approval ratings are down in the 30s.' They're falling. On some issues, they're in the 20s. This is bad, bad news coming up to an election, and Susie Wiles is the shock absorber who gets those calls," he said, as a new poll on Monday showed the president sinking to just 29 percent approval. "So I'm sure she is super unhappy with this. I can't imagine she and Natalie are besties," Rothkopf said. "But frankly, the other sycophants in the White House all want to be up in Trump's drawers like Natalie. I think they're jealous. You know, I think everybody's jealous of the fact that this 35-year-old woman has found the inside track to the president by playing to his absolute obsession with how he is covered in the media." Banning the three networks was also a "bad idea" Rothkopf said, because it didn't turn out well when the Trump administration revoked then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press pass. "The last term he did it to Jim Acosta of CNN, who went to court and got his pass reinstated because, you know, there is the First Amendment still. But nonetheless, Trump has done this. And it finally moved one of the slowest-responding, most pusillanimous organizations in Washington to action—which is to say White House correspondents—because they have watched week in and week out as he has abused women, particularly Kaitlan Collins of CNN and others, and they haven't done anything. But finally this was a straw too much." The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. extraction.body: The newly minted MAGA-approved TV pool appears to have inadvertently made itself a security risk for the president. The pro-Trump outlet Real America’s Voice became the primary television crew traveling with President Donald Trump to the United Nations General Assembly this week after he banned CNN, which was scheduled to provide a pool feed from New York on Monday, from the White House. Real America’s Voice, now tasked with providing footage to media partners, shared footage from inside Trump’s motorcade as he was driven off of the UN campus and out of New York. The video was hailed by online MAGA flacks, including Nick Sortor, who said he was grateful to Real America’s Voice for “showing us RAW footage of how difficult it is to keep President Trump safe.” In reality, they may have breached an all-important protocol. Former White House Correspondents’ Association President Weijia Jiang of CBS News poured cold water on the apparent access the public was getting. “For decades, the [WHCA] has advised poolers not to air video of taillights because it’s a potential risk to the security of the motorcade,” she said. Several big-name journalists endorsed her post, including ABC’s Jonathan Karl, CNN’s Brian Stelter, and Face the Nation host Margaret Breman, among others. Former WHCA President Kelly O’Donnell of NBC News echoed the sentiment, posting that the association has “long provided specific guidance from the Secret Service and various administrations on matters where video material should not be used at all or with limitations for security reasons.” Each presidential motorcade features at least two identical Cadillac limousines, each displaying the presidential seal and American flags, which is intended to make it impossible for the average spectator to know which vehicle is carrying the president. Their footage from inside the motorcade shows the New York Police Department escorting the presidential motorcade out of the UN campus and onto a New York City highway. With Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, the other networks responsible for TV pool duty—ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox—have said they will stand in solidarity with their media colleagues and not honor their scheduled pool coverage. That means pool coverage has fallen to MAGA media outlets like Real America’s Voice and Lindell TV, which is owned by the 2020 election denier Mike Lindell. Performance One Media, a Colorado-based media company run by Robert Sigg, owns Real America’s Voice. Sigg appears to be a more unsavory character, as he has gotten in trouble with the law for domestic violence, burglary, drug distribution, driving under the influence, and assault, charges that were later dropped. He also has a white-collar crime track record, having pleaded guilty to one count of bank fraud stemming from his role in a $19 million mortgage-fraud scheme. In 2013, his son, Austin, was sentenced to life in prison at age 17 in 2013 for kidnapping and murdering 10-year-old Jessica Ridgeway. Sigg’s outlet is best-known for airing Steve Bannon’s War Room show. The same day the major networks announced they were standing with CNN in solidarity, the White House tried to fight back by launching what it called “TRUMP TV,” which airs round the clock. It has tried to sell the programming as giving people the ability to “watch the Trump Administration’s biggest moments all in one place.” But there appears to be little interest in the new venture, as live viewership has been as low as 500 people on YouTube.

extraction.body: Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At Connect on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market. These glasses actually seem quite promising given their substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility. Moments before unveiling the VR glasses, MEta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile back to focus less on Metaverse and to build fewer VR devices until it has real breakthroughs. “This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.” The company says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal glasses than the bulky headsets that Meta previously released. Made of magnesium alloy, the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They are powered by a computing puck, which also acts as their battery. Presumably, a user can just slip the puck into their pocket, which allows the glasses to be used on the go. The glasses are largely entertainment-focused and come with micro-OLED panels built into the lenses, which provide a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, as well as Dolby Vision and support for Dolby Atmos audio. Users will be able to download and watch movies. Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films. Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever.” What does that mean? Meta maintains that their glasses will be one of the only ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines the distinct high-resolution viewing experience. The glasses are also compatible with 3D experiences — and even movies that integrate a user’s physical space is integrated into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that, in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D. Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience. Moments before unveiling the VR glasses, MEta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile back to focus less on Metaverse and to build fewer VR devices until it has real breakthroughs.

“This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. passages: In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset.
Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas.
Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9.

A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles.
The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it.

Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie.

Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.
The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets.
Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock.

However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around.

Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.
That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer.
There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled.
Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby.

extraction.body: Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie. Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor. “We are… self-aware,” she sighed. A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles. The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it. However, the reveal of Meta’s new entertainment-centric gizmo, Meta VR Glasses, arriving this spring, might just be enough of a departure to entice agonistics like myself, starting with the fact that wearing them doesn’t make you feel like you’re in an episode of Black Mirror. They are, for all intents and purposes, a pair of slick dark glasses. They still have the noticeable bulge of a VR device, but they’re more along the lines of X-Men’s Cyclops than Johnny Mnemonic . These streamlined shades feature a cable leading to a “puck” the size of an iPhone, a battery-and-computer pack you can place in your pocket or handbag, or clip to your belt. Its 45W fast-charging will probably come in handy, since it only holds enough juice for three hours of continuous playback, but the dangling accessory isn’t too obtrusive a trade-off, given the device’s larger, heavier predecessors. The glasses themselves weigh only about a hundred grams — a quarter of a pound — compared to the five to six hundred grams of the Meta Quest. The biggest upgrade from the Meta Quest, however, is the complete lack of hand-held controllers and the reliance on physical gestures instead. Apple’s equivalent already has this, but the Meta VR Glasses offer the chance to use these flicks and pinches without feeling like you’re in a Saw trap. The initial adjustments seem pretty easy, between switchable nose pads of different sizes and lenses you can slide left and right to ensure they’re at the correct distance. There’s no official info on what to do if you wear glasses just yet, but some leaks out there suggest prescription lens capability is the plan. Tiny cameras alongside the glasses' stems capture minor movements, like using your thumb to imitate scrolling on a touch remote, or pinching an invisible button, which in turn trigger and toggle menus affixed to the space around you. The cameras on the front re-create your regular vision, with a bit of a catch. The world around you gets noticeably noisier (as in, filled with digital noise) and the frame rate doesn’t exactly sync up with fluorescent lightbulbs, so you might see a bit of a flicker when looking past the floating UX at actual surfaces. Navigating the real world will still probably be a challenge, and the tech’s hologram features (and spatial audio) for video calling weren’t part of the demo. However, Meta VR Glasses feel aimed at sitting down to watch movies and TV rather than augmenting reality. With its 5K display made of micro OLED panels, 37 pixels per degree, and Dolby Vision enhancements, you’re getting a pretty high-quality image, and navigating it is gamified too. Once you sync your eye movements to the cursor, simply looking at an app icon will light it up. Just pinch to select. But what about the actual offerings? Well, that’s where things get interesting. In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset. Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9. With films like The Odyssey , Sinners and Dune: Part Three reflecting an increased demand for the format, which can’t fully be met, this is the next best thing. But what does actually watching a movie in one of these look like? Well, you have a couple of options. For most films, a screen pops up at a certain distance, which you’ll eventually be able to move back or forth. This feature wasn’t yet available, leaving part of the screen outside the glasses’ field of view, which isn’t ideal, but it’s still early days since the product is several months away from release. Your second option, for select films and experiences, is an “Immersive Cinema” virtual reality viewing room by ILM, built in sync with the movie itself. For this Disney+ demo, I picked Avengers: Infinity War — specifically, the scene where Thor harnesses the power of a dying star to forge his new hammer, Stormbreaker. If you’ve ever fantasized about watching a movie while seated in a grungy space factory as lava splashes from around the screen, you’re in luck. For Marvel and Star Wars offerings, environments like Tatooine and Avengers Tower appear to be in the works. The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets. Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock. However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around. This isn’t magic; the folks at Meta had cameras appropriately placed to capture the effect, so future games will have to be equipped for this sort of broadcast if you want to, say, wave at Spike Lee as he jumps around euphorically. Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through. The speakers on the glasses — which you can control using tiny buttons along the bottoms of the stems — provide a fairly immersive surround sound experience courtesy of Dolby Atmos. This comes in handy for playing music-based games like Beat Saber, one of 75 built-in games available at launch (this particular version was enhanced for the device’s handsfree capabilities) in addition to the XBOX Cloud Gaming, i.e. streaming games directly to your headset. You also have the option of scrolling social media, and typing on a nifty keyboard projected on flat surfaces in front of you, as you look down at your digital ghost hands and their spectral glow. The novelty will probably wear off after a while, but at first, it’s pretty thrilling if you’ve never used this kind of technology before — which appears to be the target market for Meta VR Glasses. Of course, there’s a work capability too; you can mirror your Mac or PC into this virtual space, either wirelessly or via USB-C. On the other hand, the device’s $1,299.99 price tag — more than a solid TV and Blu-ray player combined — might be a deterrent to the average consumer who hasn’t yet dipped their toe into VR. That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer. The only way to be remotely convinced of the technology is to experience it for yourself, which a re-creation on a flat screen (say, a YouTube video) can’t fully convey. There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled. There are kinks that still need to be worked out by launch, like the glare from light sources behind you leaking into your field of view (perhaps the one downside to opening up those goggles), but a head tilt here or there can probably solve that issue. Also not part of the tech demo was the ability to re-orient where exactly in your horizontal field of view a given screen appears, but this was something Meta’s engineers demonstrated for us on the fly, with the promise that we’d eventually be able to do it ourselves. Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby. Look, it can be hard to trust big tech in our increasingly dystopian world, and who knows what data this particular chapter of the company will try to harness or sell. But the lineup of streaming services and viewing features on offer makes Meta VR Glasses one of the more intriguing developments in the field if you’re unsure about stepping into virtual spaces. Compared to existing devices on the market, the openness of the design — which still allows you to peek out from time to time and go back to the real world pretty easily — makes for the kind of compromise that fence-sitters like myself might just be able to accept. If nothing else, it’s more convenient, and slightly less embarrassing, than buying a scalped IMAX ticket on eBay.

The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it.

Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie.

Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.

However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around.

Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.
That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer.
There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled.
Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby.

These glasses actually seem quite promising given their substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility. Moments before unveiling the VR glasses, MEta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile back to focus less on Metaverse and to build fewer VR devices until it has real breakthroughs. “This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.” The company says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal glasses than the bulky headsets that Meta previously released. Made of magnesium alloy, the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They are powered by a computing puck, which also acts as their battery. Presumably, a user can just slip the puck into their pocket, which allows the glasses to be used on the go. The glasses are largely entertainment-focused and come with micro-OLED panels built into the lenses, which provide a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, as well as Dolby Vision and support for Dolby Atmos audio. Users will be able to download and watch movies. Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films. Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever.” What does that mean? Meta maintains that their glasses will be one of the only ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines the distinct high-resolution viewing experience. The glasses are also compatible with 3D experiences — and even movies that integrate a user’s physical space is integrated into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that, in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D. Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience. The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures. extraction.body: Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie. Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor. “We are… self-aware,” she sighed. A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles. The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it. However, the reveal of Meta’s new entertainment-centric gizmo, Meta VR Glasses, arriving this spring, might just be enough of a departure to entice agonistics like myself, starting with the fact that wearing them doesn’t make you feel like you’re in an episode of Black Mirror. They are, for all intents and purposes, a pair of slick dark glasses. They still have the noticeable bulge of a VR device, but they’re more along the lines of X-Men’s Cyclops than Johnny Mnemonic . These streamlined shades feature a cable leading to a “puck” the size of an iPhone, a battery-and-computer pack you can place in your pocket or handbag, or clip to your belt. Its 45W fast-charging will probably come in handy, since it only holds enough juice for three hours of continuous playback, but the dangling accessory isn’t too obtrusive a trade-off, given the device’s larger, heavier predecessors. The glasses themselves weigh only about a hundred grams — a quarter of a pound — compared to the five to six hundred grams of the Meta Quest. The biggest upgrade from the Meta Quest, however, is the complete lack of hand-held controllers and the reliance on physical gestures instead. Apple’s equivalent already has this, but the Meta VR Glasses offer the chance to use these flicks and pinches without feeling like you’re in a Saw trap. The initial adjustments seem pretty easy, between switchable nose pads of different sizes and lenses you can slide left and right to ensure they’re at the correct distance. There’s no official info on what to do if you wear glasses just yet, but some leaks out there suggest prescription lens capability is the plan. Tiny cameras alongside the glasses' stems capture minor movements, like using your thumb to imitate scrolling on a touch remote, or pinching an invisible button, which in turn trigger and toggle menus affixed to the space around you. The cameras on the front re-create your regular vision, with a bit of a catch. The world around you gets noticeably noisier (as in, filled with digital noise) and the frame rate doesn’t exactly sync up with fluorescent lightbulbs, so you might see a bit of a flicker when looking past the floating UX at actual surfaces. Navigating the real world will still probably be a challenge, and the tech’s hologram features (and spatial audio) for video calling weren’t part of the demo. However, Meta VR Glasses feel aimed at sitting down to watch movies and TV rather than augmenting reality. With its 5K display made of micro OLED panels, 37 pixels per degree, and Dolby Vision enhancements, you’re getting a pretty high-quality image, and navigating it is gamified too. Once you sync your eye movements to the cursor, simply looking at an app icon will light it up. Just pinch to select. But what about the actual offerings? Well, that’s where things get interesting. In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset. Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9. With films like The Odyssey , Sinners and Dune: Part Three reflecting an increased demand for the format, which can’t fully be met, this is the next best thing. But what does actually watching a movie in one of these look like? Well, you have a couple of options. For most films, a screen pops up at a certain distance, which you’ll eventually be able to move back or forth. This feature wasn’t yet available, leaving part of the screen outside the glasses’ field of view, which isn’t ideal, but it’s still early days since the product is several months away from release. Your second option, for select films and experiences, is an “Immersive Cinema” virtual reality viewing room by ILM, built in sync with the movie itself. For this Disney+ demo, I picked Avengers: Infinity War — specifically, the scene where Thor harnesses the power of a dying star to forge his new hammer, Stormbreaker. If you’ve ever fantasized about watching a movie while seated in a grungy space factory as lava splashes from around the screen, you’re in luck. For Marvel and Star Wars offerings, environments like Tatooine and Avengers Tower appear to be in the works. The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets. Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock. However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around. This isn’t magic; the folks at Meta had cameras appropriately placed to capture the effect, so future games will have to be equipped for this sort of broadcast if you want to, say, wave at Spike Lee as he jumps around euphorically. Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through. The speakers on the glasses — which you can control using tiny buttons along the bottoms of the stems — provide a fairly immersive surround sound experience courtesy of Dolby Atmos. This comes in handy for playing music-based games like Beat Saber, one of 75 built-in games available at launch (this particular version was enhanced for the device’s handsfree capabilities) in addition to the XBOX Cloud Gaming, i.e. streaming games directly to your headset. You also have the option of scrolling social media, and typing on a nifty keyboard projected on flat surfaces in front of you, as you look down at your digital ghost hands and their spectral glow. The novelty will probably wear off after a while, but at first, it’s pretty thrilling if you’ve never used this kind of technology before — which appears to be the target market for Meta VR Glasses. Of course, there’s a work capability too; you can mirror your Mac or PC into this virtual space, either wirelessly or via USB-C. On the other hand, the device’s $1,299.99 price tag — more than a solid TV and Blu-ray player combined — might be a deterrent to the average consumer who hasn’t yet dipped their toe into VR. That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer. The only way to be remotely convinced of the technology is to experience it for yourself, which a re-creation on a flat screen (say, a YouTube video) can’t fully convey. There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled. There are kinks that still need to be worked out by launch, like the glare from light sources behind you leaking into your field of view (perhaps the one downside to opening up those goggles), but a head tilt here or there can probably solve that issue. Also not part of the tech demo was the ability to re-orient where exactly in your horizontal field of view a given screen appears, but this was something Meta’s engineers demonstrated for us on the fly, with the promise that we’d eventually be able to do it ourselves. Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby. Look, it can be hard to trust big tech in our increasingly dystopian world, and who knows what data this particular chapter of the company will try to harness or sell. But the lineup of streaming services and viewing features on offer makes Meta VR Glasses one of the more intriguing developments in the field if you’re unsure about stepping into virtual spaces. Compared to existing devices on the market, the openness of the design — which still allows you to peek out from time to time and go back to the real world pretty easily — makes for the kind of compromise that fence-sitters like myself might just be able to accept. If nothing else, it’s more convenient, and slightly less embarrassing, than buying a scalped IMAX ticket on eBay.

sources.title: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features
passages: OpenAI announced on Wednesday that it is bringing voice-based agentic features to mobile, allowing users to trigger workflows like drafting documents or summarizing emails.
OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will have richer text output.
Plus, users will be able to switch between text and voice easily.
They can also start working on a conversation on the go and resume it on desktop.
These subscribers can do things like build sites, create presentations, use the cloud browser, and also access other areas like finances in ChatGPT.
The feature arrives as an increasing number of users are turning to voice to issue commands to AI assistants for complex tasks.

sources.title: ChatGPT Mobile App Adds Voice-Based Agentic Features - entARABI
passages: OpenAI is expanding the capabilities of the ChatGPT mobile app with new voice-based agentic features that allow users to carry out more complex tasks using voice commands.
The mobile rollout follows the launch of OpenAI’s conversational voice model, GPT-Live , in July 2026.
OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will also provide richer text output, creating a more seamless experience between spoken and written interactions.
The model was introduced to make voice conversations with ChatGPT feel more natural and interactive.
The latest update brings similar capabilities to mobile devices as voice increasingly becomes a way to control AI assistants and execute multi-step tasks.

extraction.body: Meta Connect 2026 is right around the corner. Like other annual tech events, such as Made by Google or Apple's fall event, Connect is Meta's chance to showcase the hardware and AI tools it plans to launch over the next year. The company may have started as a single social media platform, but it now dominates or competes in multiple tech fields, including virtual reality headsets, LLMs, and, as of late, personal AI agents, thanks to the introduction of Muse AI. Here's what I'm expecting to see at Meta Connect 2026. Could Meta's new smart glasses be more privacy-friendly?While the company will undoubtedly announce new AI developments this week, Meta Connect 2026 will likely also make headlines for its hardware division. Meta is well known (perhaps infamous) for its smart glasses, so it only makes sense that the company would make relevant announcements during a major tech event. But the most newsworthy moment of all might not be an "advancement," so much as a refinement. As PCMag reports, Meta is planning to announce camera-free smart glasses at Connect 2026. These glasses, codenamed "Luna," would rely on an array of six microphones rather than cameras to power AI features. That way, you could still ask Meta AI questions or give commands to Muse AI, without the need for cameras to tap into the world around you. Meta's most popular smart glasses currently come with embedded cameras, so why the change? It's probably not to offer users a "budget" smart glasses option. Instead, it's more likely that Meta is responding to growing backlash over its current camera-enabled smart glasses. It turns out that, as popular as these glasses are, a lot of people don't like the idea of being stealthily recorded anywhere they go. The problem was made worse by an underground industry of hackers aiming to disable the recording light on Meta smart glasses, making it even harder to know whether someone was sneakily filming you. To its credit, Meta has already responded to these "critiques." The company reportedly patched the exploit hackers were taking advantage of, so users shouldn't be able to bypass the recording light any longer: If the LED is blocked, Meta smart glasses are now supposed to disable video recording. Introducing camera-free smart glasses may be another step in that direction, but that won't change the fact that camera-embedded smart glasses are still readily accessible and easy to miss in passing. While there are steps individuals can take to protect their privacy in the face of these cameras, it's really an uphill battle. It's not just smart glasses giving Meta PR trouble. The company recently settled a massive lawsuit for nearly $18 billion, ending legal action from most of the states. The lawsuit alleged that Meta's platforms were harmful and addictive to children and teens, and in addition to financial compensation, Meta is now changing its rules for underage users on its platforms. That comes just ahead of the release of The Social Reckoning, a movie dramatizing Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen's revelations about the company in The Wall Street Journal's "The Facebook Files" investigation. Meta also recently backtracked on an Instagram feature that let anyone generate AI images from your public photos. Meta Connect 2026 could be a bit of a reset for Meta in a rather unforgiving environment. Meta could finally announce its "Phoenix" mixed reality "glasses"Meta could also take the opportunity to announce its long-rumored "Phoenix" mixed reality "glasses." Why the quotes? If rumors are to be believed, this device will be more of a headset than Meta's current smart glasses offerings, employing a goggles-like design, or perhaps something that looks like a "bulky pair of glasses."That said, the expectation is that Phoenix will be more portable and practical than Meta Quest, the company's VR headset. Phoenix may use an external "compute puck" to handle advanced processes, which would allow the headset to be lighter than it otherwise might be. All the while, it could run HorizonOS, the same operating system Meta Quest headsets run. You might get the best of both worlds: A high-quality mixed reality experience without the need for a bulky headset.Meta may announce AI news and updatesAs much as Meta Connect will likely focus on hardware, AI will also probably take up much of the presentation. Expect more updates about Muse AI, the company's new AI agent that can perform tasks on your behalf—even if Meta simply takes the opportunity to promote the feature. Meta may also announce a new version of Llama, the company's flagship AI model, which hasn't been updated since April of 2025, though I haven't seen any rumors about this specifically. How to watch Meta Connect 2026Meta Connect 2026 spans two days: Sept. You should be able to access the livestream from Meta Connect's official site, though the stream isn't accessible at this time. (Meta has an option to "register" for the livestream, but it seems designed to send you an alert when the livestream is available.)

extraction.body: Meta Connect 2026 is right around the corner. Like other annual tech events, such as Made by Google or Apple's fall event, Connect is Meta's chance to showcase the hardware and AI tools it plans to launch over the next year. The company may have started as a single social media platform, but it now dominates or competes in multiple tech fields, including virtual reality headsets, LLMs, and, as of late, personal AI agents, thanks to the introduction of Muse AI. Here's what I'm expecting to see at Meta Connect 2026. Could Meta's new smart glasses be more privacy-friendly?While the company will undoubtedly announce new AI developments this week, Meta Connect 2026 will likely also make headlines for its hardware division. Meta is well known (perhaps infamous) for its smart glasses, so it only makes sense that the company would make relevant announcements during a major tech event. But the most newsworthy moment of all might not be an "advancement," so much as a refinement. As PCMag reports, Meta is planning to announce camera-free smart glasses at Connect 2026. These glasses, codenamed "Luna," would rely on an array of six microphones rather than cameras to power AI features. That way, you could still ask Meta AI questions or give commands to Muse AI, without the need for cameras to tap into the world around you. Meta's most popular smart glasses currently come with embedded cameras, so why the change? It's probably not to offer users a "budget" smart glasses option. Instead, it's more likely that Meta is responding to growing backlash over its current camera-enabled smart glasses. It turns out that, as popular as these glasses are, a lot of people don't like the idea of being stealthily recorded anywhere they go. The problem was made worse by an underground industry of hackers aiming to disable the recording light on Meta smart glasses, making it even harder to know whether someone was sneakily filming you. To its credit, Meta has already responded to these "critiques." The company reportedly patched the exploit hackers were taking advantage of, so users shouldn't be able to bypass the recording light any longer: If the LED is blocked, Meta smart glasses are now supposed to disable video recording. Introducing camera-free smart glasses may be another step in that direction, but that won't change the fact that camera-embedded smart glasses are still readily accessible and easy to miss in passing. While there are steps individuals can take to protect their privacy in the face of these cameras, it's really an uphill battle. It's not just smart glasses giving Meta PR trouble. The company recently settled a massive lawsuit for nearly $18 billion, ending legal action from most of the states. The lawsuit alleged that Meta's platforms were harmful and addictive to children and teens, and in addition to financial compensation, Meta is now changing its rules for underage users on its platforms. That comes just ahead of the release of The Social Reckoning, a movie dramatizing Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen's revelations about the company in The Wall Street Journal's "The Facebook Files" investigation. Meta also recently backtracked on an Instagram feature that let anyone generate AI images from your public photos. Meta Connect 2026 could be a bit of a reset for Meta in a rather unforgiving environment. Meta could finally announce its "Phoenix" mixed reality "glasses"Meta could also take the opportunity to announce its long-rumored "Phoenix" mixed reality "glasses." Why the quotes? If rumors are to be believed, this device will be more of a headset than Meta's current smart glasses offerings, employing a goggles-like design, or perhaps something that looks like a "bulky pair of glasses."That said, the expectation is that Phoenix will be more portable and practical than Meta Quest, the company's VR headset. Phoenix may use an external "compute puck" to handle advanced processes, which would allow the headset to be lighter than it otherwise might be. All the while, it could run HorizonOS, the same operating system Meta Quest headsets run. You might get the best of both worlds: A high-quality mixed reality experience without the need for a bulky headset.Meta may announce AI news and updatesAs much as Meta Connect will likely focus on hardware, AI will also probably take up much of the presentation. Expect more updates about Muse AI, the company's new AI agent that can perform tasks on your behalf—even if Meta simply takes the opportunity to promote the feature. Meta may also announce a new version of Llama, the company's flagship AI model, which hasn't been updated since April of 2025, though I haven't seen any rumors about this specifically. How to watch Meta Connect 2026Meta Connect 2026 spans two days: Sept. You should be able to access the livestream from Meta Connect's official site, though the stream isn't accessible at this time. (Meta has an option to "register" for the livestream, but it seems designed to send you an alert when the livestream is available.)

extraction.body: President Donald Trump speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026, in New York City. Getty Images / Michael M. Santiago President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced a rebranding of the term “artificial intelligence,” saying during the United Nations General Assembly that from now on, it will be called “super intelligence.” “From this point forward, all of United States’ documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, ‘super,’ as opposed to ‘artificial’,” he said. Though the rebrand may have been a surprise to many, superintelligence is already an established term in AI literature. It was popularized in philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2014 bestseller Superintelligence , which defines the term as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.” Artificial superintelligence, or ASI, thus refers to future AI systems that could be much smarter than humans, and contrasts with the weaker forms of AI that exist today. ASI is a step beyond AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which OpenAI defines as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” By this definition, today’s AI isn’t AGI yet, much less ASI, since we can’t yet hire AI as a reliable virtual employee. Some experts dislike the term superintelligence, or question whether it’s a coherent concept. In the influential 2025 paper “AI as Normal Technology,” authors Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan write, “We do not think there is a useful sense of the term ‘intelligence’ in which AI is more intelligent than people acting with the help of AI.” But others say the possible renaming contributes to an ongoing conversation about AI’s growing abilities. “‘Super’ does align well with the fact that AI is exceeding human capabilities in a growing range of tasks and by increasing margins, which can have distinct national security implications beyond simply matching human performance,” said Caleb Withers, a research associate for the Technology and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. For example, in early September, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, one of the most important open problems in math. As AI becomes more capable, it has grown increasingly central to the U.S.-China relationship. Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are slated to meet this week to discuss trade and AI issues. Bostrom, who has warned of the dangers of fully superintelligent AI systems, said an all-out AI race increases the risk that the technology gets out of control . “If competitors are convinced that coming second [in the AI race] means the total loss of everything they care about, they will take whatever risk necessary to bypass their rivals,” he said. Trump reportedly worries that an AI slowdown could cause a market crash, and sees “super intelligence” as a critical sector for America to stay ahead of China. “Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins.” NEXT STORY: NATO’s thumbs-up for AWS shows Europe still needs America

President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced a rebranding of the term “artificial intelligence,” saying during the United Nations General Assembly that from now on, it will be called “super intelligence.”
“From this point forward, all of United States’ documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, ‘super,’ as opposed to ‘artificial’,” he said.

Though the rebrand may have been a surprise to many, superintelligence is already an established term in AI literature. It was popularized in philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2014 bestseller Superintelligence , which defines the term as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.” Artificial superintelligence, or ASI, thus refers to future AI systems that could be much smarter than humans, and contrasts with the weaker forms of AI that exist today.

ASI is a step beyond AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which OpenAI defines as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” By this definition, today’s AI isn’t AGI yet, much less ASI, since we can’t yet hire AI as a reliable virtual employee.

Some experts dislike the term superintelligence, or question whether it’s a coherent concept. In the influential 2025 paper “AI as Normal Technology,” authors Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan write, “We do not think there is a useful sense of the term ‘intelligence’ in which AI is more intelligent than people acting with the help of AI.”
But others say the possible renaming contributes to an ongoing conversation about AI’s growing abilities.

“‘Super’ does align well with the fact that AI is exceeding human capabilities in a growing range of tasks and by increasing margins, which can have distinct national security implications beyond simply matching human performance,” said Caleb Withers, a research associate for the Technology and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
For example, in early September, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, one of the most important open problems in math.

As AI becomes more capable, it has grown increasingly central to the U.S.-China relationship. Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are slated to meet this week to discuss trade and AI issues. Bostrom, who has warned of the dangers of fully superintelligent AI systems, said an all-out AI race increases the risk that the technology gets out of control . “If competitors are convinced that coming second [in the AI race] means the total loss of everything they care about, they will take whatever risk necessary to bypass their rivals,” he said.

Trump reportedly worries that an AI slowdown could cause a market crash, and sees “super intelligence” as a critical sector for America to stay ahead of China. “Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins.”
